prompt.context: Consider a law firm. They hire in associates right out of law school at $100,000 a year.
prompt.question: Is hiring a new associate at $100,000 per year a good deal for the law firm?

clarifying_info.q: Does the firm have enough work to keep a new associate busy?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, assume the firm has work for the new associate.

clarifying_info.q: What is the billing rate for a new associate?
clarifying_info.a: Candidate should estimate; typical new-associate rates range from $150 to $300+ per hour.

clarifying_info.q: How many hours does an associate bill per day?
clarifying_info.a: Candidate should estimate; typically 6-8 billable hours per day.

clarifying_info.q: How many days per year does an associate work?
clarifying_info.a: Candidate should estimate; roughly 250 working days per year.

clarifying_info.q: What costs beyond salary should we consider?
clarifying_info.a: Candidate should brainstorm: taxes, benefits, overhead, training, recruiting costs, etc.

framework: Step 1 — Marginal Revenue: Estimate the annual revenue generated by the new associate (hourly billing rate x billable hours per day x working days per year).
Step 2 — Marginal Costs: Identify all incremental costs beyond the $100K salary (taxes, benefits, overhead, training, recruiting costs amortized over expected tenure).
Step 3 — Profit Check: Calculate profit = revenue - total costs; determine whether the hire is profitable.
Step 4 — Qualitative Factors: Assess whether $100K is above or below market, the need for raises in subsequent years, and alternatives (experienced lawyers, legal assistants).

questions.prompt: Estimate the annual revenue a new associate generates for the firm.
questions.guidance: Walk through assumptions clearly: billing rate (e.g., $200/hr), billable hours per day (e.g., 7 hrs), working days per year (e.g., 250). Revenue = $200 x 7 x 250 = $350,000. Candidate should state assumptions explicitly and check whether the number is reasonable.

math.setup: Annual Revenue = billing rate x billable hours per day x working days per year
steps: Assume billable hours per day = 7 hrs
Assume working days per year = 250 days

questions.prompt: Estimate the full incremental cost of the new associate beyond the base salary.
questions.guidance: Candidate should enumerate cost categories: payroll taxes (~15% of salary = $15K), benefits (~20% = $20K), overhead/office space (~$20-30K), training (~$10K), recruiting costs amortized over tenure (e.g., $20K recruiting fee / 3-year average tenure = ~$7K/yr). Total additional costs roughly $70-80K on top of $100K salary, giving total cost ~$170-180K.

math.setup: Total Cost = salary + taxes + benefits + overhead + training + amortized recruiting

questions.prompt: Is hiring the associate a good deal? What is the profit margin?
questions.guidance: Profit = Revenue - Total Cost = $350,000 - $177,000 = $173,000. Profit margin = $173K / $350K ≈ 49%. This is a good deal assuming the associate is fully utilized. Candidate should also note sensitivity of the answer to billing rate and utilization assumptions.

math.setup: Profit = Revenue - Total Cost; Margin = Profit / Revenue
math.answer: Profit ≈ $173,000; margin ≈ 49% — a good deal if associate is fully utilized

brainstorming.prompt: What other factors or alternatives should the firm consider when deciding whether to hire an associate at $100,000?

categories.name: Pricing & Market Benchmarking
ideas: Is $100K above or below market rate for new law school graduates?
Would paying above-market attract higher-quality talent that generates more revenue?

categories.name: Career Progression & Raises
ideas: Associates will demand raises in subsequent years — model salary trajectory
Consider the cost of retaining vs. replacing associates who are promoted or leave

categories.name: Alternative Staffing Options
ideas: Hire experienced lateral lawyers who can bill at higher rates immediately
Use paralegals or legal assistants for routine work at lower cost
Outsource specific tasks (document review, research) at lower hourly cost

categories.name: Utilization Risk
ideas: Revenue estimate assumes full utilization — what if workload is insufficient?
Overhead is largely fixed; underutilized associates erode margin quickly

categories.name: Indirect Benefits
ideas: New associates can free up partner time, allowing partners to focus on high-value work
Building associate pipeline supports future partner promotion and firm growth

recommendation: Based on the analysis, hiring a new associate at $100,000 is a good deal: estimated revenue of ~$350K versus total cost of ~$177K yields ~$173K in profit and a ~49% margin.
The hire creates value as long as the associate maintains high billable-hour utilization and billing rates stay at or above market.
risks: Utilization risk — if the associate bills fewer hours the economics deteriorate rapidly
Rising salary expectations in years 2-3 will compress margins unless billing rates keep pace
Recruiting and training costs are upfront; the firm absorbs them before the associate is productive
next_steps: Verify current market salary and billing rate benchmarks for new associates in this market
Model a multi-year P&L including raises and promotion milestones
Evaluate whether demand (billable work) supports adding headcount before committing to hire
